entries.title: Why US investors are snapping up Germany's famed Mittelstand
entries.summary: Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.
entries.content:
October 20, 2026

Increasing amounts of US capital are flowing into Germany's traditional industrial firms and family-owned businesses. As many business owners struggle to find successors, more companies are becoming acquisition targets.

What do the long-established German companies Birkenstock, Viessmann, Linde and ebm-papst have in common? All have fallen into American hands.

Traditional German family-owned businesses and small-to-medium-sized enterprises (SMEs) have become increasingly attractive to US companies and investors.

Last year, US investors were involved in 76 acquisitions and investments in German industrial and manufacturing companies, according to an analysis by financial data provider PitchBook. The transactions were valued at about $29.5 billion (€26.3 billion) in 2025, nearly double the 2022 total. As of August 19, 2026, the figure stood at $23.9 billion.

No successor, but an investor instead

"From what we are seeing in the market, the interest from US investors in German companies is definitely still there," said Samar-Ahmad Albrecht-Mahmood of Veracity Capital Investments, which advises companies looking to invest in Germany.

German companies, particularly those in the industrial and manufacturing sector, remain attractive, "because many of them are highly specialized, have strong customer relationships and very good technical know-how," he told DW. "In many cases, these are businesses that have built up a strong position in their niche over decades."

At the same time, many German business owners are reaching an age where they are thinking about selling their business, Albrecht-Mahmood underscored, pointing out that "there is often no successor within the family."

"This brings companies onto the market that might not have been available for sale a few years ago," he said.

Notable takeovers this year include ebm-papst, the Mulfingen-based manufacturer of electric motors and fans, which was bought by US company Madison Air for $5.4 billion in August.

In June, the long-established Augsburg-based company Everllence, formerly MAN Energy Solutions, was sold to Bain Capital, with the US investment firm acquiring a 51% stake in the company.

Fewer acquisitions, but more investments

According to Die Deutsche Wirtschaft (DDW), a German business information network focused on the Mittelstand (medium-sized and family-owned companies), no country owns more German firms than the United States. Of the total 7,861 companies identified in the database "German Companies Under Foreign Ownership," 1,750 are currently held by US investors.

PricewaterhouseCoopers (PwC), one of the world's leading auditing and consultancy organizations, also underscored the growing US investor interest in acquiring German companies. In a report, titled Destination Germany, PwC said that while the number of acquisitions and equity investments has not increased, the financial volume of the deals has jumped.

The report highlighted, in particular, the acquisition of BASF Coatings by the US investment firm Carlyle, in partnership with the Qatar Investment Authority (QIA), for around €7.7 billion.

The deal was struck on October 26, 2025, and closed on June 30 of this year.

Waiting for reforms

According to a recent survey by the American Chamber of Commerce in Germany, about 62% of the US companies active in the country are expecting business conditions to improve over the next three to four years.

Meanwhile, some 52% of them are planning to expand their operations in Germany, up from 49% in 2024.

At first glance, however, the increase in US acquisitions and equity investments does not seem to align with the decline in US investment flows to Germany last year.

According to the Bundesbank, significantly less investment capital flowed from the US to Germany in 2025 than in the previous year.

While foreign direct investment in Germany has risen overall — from €57.4 billion in 2024 to a total of €86.1 billion last year — investment from the US amounted to only €11.8 billion, nearly 44% less than in 2024.

In contrast, investment from the United Kingdom rose to around €26 billion.

"I would say the trend is continuing, although perhaps not simply in terms of higher deal numbers every year," Albrecht-Mahmood said. "The general interest in good German industrial companies, especially strong Mittelstand businesses, remains high."

Relatively low valuations also play a role, the expert argued. "Compared to the US, we still see situations where German companies are valued more moderately, particularly in the SME segment. This can make acquisitions quite attractive for international buyers."

This article was originally written in German.

entries.title: Brutal, revolutionary empire builder: Genghis Khan's legacy
entries.summary: Berlin is host to a major exhibition on the founder of the Mongol Empire and his successors. Here's how Genghis Khan disrupted the course of history.
entries.content:
October 20, 2026

Berlin is host to a major exhibition on the founder of the Mongol Empire and his successors. Here's how Genghis Khan disrupted the course of history.

Genghis Khan is one of history's most radical figures. A blood-thirsty invader whose conquests caused the deaths of an estimated 40 million people, he was also a visionary political thinker who established the largest contiguous land empire in history. 

The founder of the Mongolian Empire died in 1227. Ahead of the 800th anniversary of his death, Berlin's James-Simon-Galerie explores his legacy and the "Mongol Century" (1250–1350) in the exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols."

The power of a disruptive individual

The ruler remains "incredibly relevant" to this day, says Matthias Wemhoff, the director of the exhibition project.

"What the era of Genghis Khan — the 'Mongol century,' if you will — vividly demonstrates is how quickly established structures can collapse, how rapidly vast empires can vanish from the map and how swiftly the entire landscape can be utterly transformed," the archaeologist tells DW.

The charismatic leader's unprecedented impact on the world also evokes present-day disruptive individuals who are triggering sudden, unpredictable societal shifts, says Wemhoff: "There's always been this question: Are world politics shaped by individuals or rather by groups and sociological processes?"

In this case, the answer is clear, says the museum director, who also co-wrote a 2026 book on the nomadic leader.

"If Genghis Khan hadn't existed, the course of world history would truly have been entirely different — so much of it is inextricably linked to his person," Wemhoff says.

The founder of the world's largest empire

Genghis Khan was born as Temujin around the year 1162. His father, a Mongol chieftain called Yesugei, died when he was still a child. His family was abandoned by its tribe. To secure his familial position, Temujin killed his older half-brother, Bekter, when he was still a young teenager.

Thanks to his charismatic personality, he built alliances and found followers who helped him become the sole ruler on the Mongolian steppe. He formally adopted the title of Genghis Khan in 1206.

At its peak, the Mongol Empire covered approximately 24 million square kilometers (about 9.3 million square miles), stretching from China and Korea to parts of Eastern Europe and the Middle East, and accounting for over 16% of the Earth's total land area.

Wemhoff lists various innovations under his rule: For one, Genghis Khan transformed warfare. Commanders were promoted for skill, discipline and loyalty rather than based on aristocratic rank or tribal loyalties. Soldiers were organized into decimal units of 10, 100, 1,000 and 10,000.

Despite being illiterate by modern standards, he also pushed for the introduction of the first written script for the Mongolian language, which allowed to build a state bureaucracy, track population and tax registers, record decrees, issue legal decisions and handle diplomacy.

A set of laws were established that replaced fragmented tribal customs with a unified legal system.

Trade was simplified through his adoption of a paper currency.

A policy of religious freedom was also established across the Mongol Empire, allowing all individuals to practice their chosen faith without state coercion.

Before the Mongol Empire, the Silk Road was fragmented by local conflicts and heavy taxes. Mongol rule placed the entire route under a single authority, making long-distance travel vastly safer.

The Mongol Empire is known as a period of relative political stability, economic growth and cultural exchange, an era historians call the "Pax Mongolica."

But "it all came with incredible levels of cruelty. The millions of people who fell victim to the Mongols — the mass executions, the abuse of women — this happened on a scale previously unheard of," notes Wemhoff.

Shifting centers of power

The exhibition opens with a raid that happened after Genghis Khan's death, but took place just 260 kilometers (around 160 miles) away from Berlin: the 1241 Battle of Legnica, in Silesia, Poland.

It embodies the brutality and intensity of the Mongols' methods.

There came the "highly mobile, agile Mongols on small horses — lightly armored in lamellar gear, wearing helmets that left the face exposed, and wielding bows capable of firing 20 or more arrows in a single minute," points out Wemhoff.

European knights, heavily armored and mounted on large, massive warhorses, didn't stand a chance against their enemies.

"When a hail of arrows rained down on them, the horses eventually went down, and the knights ended up lying on the ground, stuck on their back, much like a June bug," he adds. "The two styles of combat were simply mismatched."

The Mongols' western campaigns shifted historic power centers in a way that still impacts world politics today.

For example, after the Mongol invasion of Kievan Rus', which was the first East Slavic state, its thriving capital Kyiv was reduced to a depopulated ruin. Moscow became a key regional power, partly because it chose to cooperate with the Mongols rather than pursue resistance.

"In our Western European collective memory, the Mongol invasion plays hardly any role. It's something of an anecdote," says Wemhoff, noting that the era of Genghis Khan and his immediate successors is barely mentioned in standard Western European school curricula.

Germans are mainly familiar with the name of the empire's founder through the 1979 Euro-disco pop band Dschingis Khan, which represented West Germany at the Eurovision Song Contest with a campy song of the same name that reduced complex history to extreme tropes.

But in eastern Europe, the Mongol invasions "changed everything fundamentally," says Wemhoff. "And so fundamentally that we still feel the consequences of it today."

The exhibition "Genghis Khan and the World of the Mongols" runs from October 21, 2026, to April 18, 2027.

Edited by Helen Whittle

entries.title: French authorities impose partial curfews in Paris, Nice
entries.summary: French authorities imposed curfews in towns and cities on Monday night after cost-of-living and anti-government protests descended into rioting and looting over the weekend. DW has the latest.
entries.content:
Published October 19, 2026last updated October 20, 2026

French authorities imposed curfews in towns and cities on Monday night after cost-of-living and anti-government protests descended into rioting and looting over the weekend. DW has the latest.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • French Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said measures introduced in several cities on Monday had "helped keep the night calm"
  • French authorities announced curfews for parts of Paris, northern cities and Nice after unrest
  • French ciwas rocked over the weekend by some of its worst rioting in recent years over amid anti-government protests
  • Italy's Meloni considering curfew after riot in Milan
  • Albania's PM says 'red line' must be drawn' after anti-government demos and clashes

Follow below for the latest on the protests and unrest in France and other parts of Europe on Tuesday, October 20:  

Skip next section French police arrest man over Limoges town hall fire

French police arrest man over Limoges town hall fire

French authorities have arrested a 40-year-old man in connection with the fire that destroyed the historic Limoges town hall during unrest over the weekend.

The building, dating from 1883, was engulfed by fire on Saturday. Its roof and belfry collapsed, making the building's destruction a symbol of the violence that accompanied nationwide protests.

The suspect was arrested by RAID, France's elite police unit, near Limoges. Prosecutors say he had previously been flagged as a potential security threat.

France's Counter-Terrorism Sub-Directorate has joined the investigation, while Justice Minister Gerald Darmanin says anti-terror prosecutors will decide whether to classify the case as a terrorist act.

Skip next section Dott, Lime count losses after Paris protesters burn shared e-Bikes

Dott, Lime count losses after Paris protesters burn shared e-Bikes

In Paris, sights of e-bikes thrown into burning piles became a common sight over the weekend, prompting bike makers Dott and Lime to asses their losses.

Shared mobility operator Dott, in a statement to Reuters on Monday, said that about 300 of its electric bikes were destroyed and 120 severely damaged in Paris, during the nationwide anti-government protests on Saturday. The company has about 6,000 bikes int he city.

Dott also said 80 vehicles, including bikes and scooters were destroyed in Bordeux and another 30-40 Scooters in Lyon. It estimates the damage at about €400,000 ($450,000).

Lime, another entity for shared electric bikes, said 6% of its Paris fleet was destroyed or damaged.

Ahead of demonstrations, Lime said it worked with the police to remove vehicles from designated protest routes and restricted parking or riding in high-risk areas.

Smovengo, operator ​of the Vélib' Métropole bike-sharing service in Paris, told Reuters that some 300 of its 20,000 bike fleet were damaged or stolen over the weekend.

E-bikes often use lithium-ion batteries that can ignite and produce intense fires and toxic smoke.

There was no indication that e-bike operators were specifically targeted during the protests. Rather, their ready availability likely played a role as protesters used them to build barricades or build fires.

Skip next section France to impose 'targeted curfews' wherever necessary, says PM

France to impose 'targeted curfews' wherever necessary, says PM

Francewill impose new curfews in areas where they are required, Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said Tuesday after the first night of partial curfews in major cities including Paris.

Lecornu said the targeted curfews had helped keep the peace overnight after a turbulent weekend that saw protesters take aim at state institutions.

"Targeted curfews have contributed to calm overnight," the premier wrote on X. "Tonight new curfews will be decided where the situation requires it. These decisions will be made on the ground, by the prefects, in coordination with the Mayors," he said.

Police confirmed the night had passed without major incidents across France.

Skip next section Trump blames immigrants, Muslims, for French unrest in attack on Democrats

Trump blames immigrants, Muslims, for French unrest in attack on Democrats

US President Donald Trump on Monday cited the unrest in France as an example while warning of what he alleged could happen in the United States if opposition Democrats were in power, without providing evidence to support the claim.

At a rally supporting the Republican Senate candidate in Kansas, Trump described France as a formerly great nation that had been "conquered, looted, and burned to the ground by migrants, jihadists and communists."

"When you see burning steeples and raging fires in France, just remember that is what ​the radical Dumocrats want to do to America," he said, using the altered version of his opponents' name that he often employs as an insult.

Ahead of the rally, Trump told reporters at the White House that he had warned French President Emmanuel Macron he was "making a big mistake."

"The whole world was coming in, and as you know, Paris is going to be a Muslim city very soon, and that wasn't the deal," he said, adding: "We closed our borders. He didn't."

The US president's return to his signature anti-immigration, anti-Muslim rhetoric, which he used to some effect in his election campaigns, comes as his party seeks to avoid a drubbing in the November midterm elections.

His comments echo previous remarks by Republican colleagues. Vice President JD Vance, for example, argued that the French protests occurred because "Western liberals imported the third world into France."

Skip next section A turbulent weekend in France: How did it come to be?

A turbulent weekend in France: How did it come to be?

Catherine Field, a journalist in Paris, told DW why demonstrations were different this time. Protests markedly sprang up in different parts of the capital city and elsewhere, particularly taking aim at state institutions. Police appeared to have lost some sense of control, she said. Listen to the full conversation here:

Skip next section READ: What has the French government said about the rioting in France?

READ: What has the French government said about the rioting in France?

French President Emmanuel Macron has vowed to punish those responsible for the rioting and violence over the weekend.

He also acknowledged "failures in anticipation and intelligence" by police and sought to make clear the distinction between rioters and demonstrators.

Skip next section Are there more protests planned in France?

Are there more protests planned in France?

The answer is yes. French unions have called for a new round of rallies on November 5.

Earlier on Monday, French President Emmanuel Macron blamed organized ultraleft groups for the rioting and looting on Saturday.

Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu said after an emergency cabinet meeting on Monday that he was "fully resolved to restore public order."

He called for imposing localized curfews, as is in place overnight into Tuesday (see below), but said there was "no question" of imposing a full curfew on entire cities.

But Lecornu refused to rule out declaring a state of emergency, which would give authorities sweeping powers to restrict public gatherings.

Skip next section Where are curfews in place in France?

Where are curfews in place in France?

Authorities in France have announced localized curfews in several areas including:

  • In northern France, including Lille, Douai, Denain and Wattignies, a curfew for minors is in place for the next two days from 8 p.m. (1800 GMT) to 6 a.m.
  • In the south, including Nice, where a specific curfew is in place for minors in the city center.
  • Two areas in Paris, where curfew prohibits anyone from entering or remaining on the Place de la République, where rioting took place Saturday, and the shopping neighborhood of Les Halles, which has been subject to looting.
  • The partial curfew in Paris went into effect at 11 p.m. Monday and remains in place until 6 a.m. Tuesday.

Skip next section Foreign governments issue France travel warnings

Foreign governments issue France travel warnings

Several countries around the world, including China, Malaysia, Germany and the United States, have advised citizens traveling to France to avoid large crowds and exercise caution in the wake of large-scale protests and looting in major cities.

China's Foreign Ministry urged Chinese nationals in France to remain alert to potential risks, increase safety precautions, and avoid ​areas where demonstrations are taking place.

Malaysia's Ministry of Foreign Affairs said that, while ⁠travel to France remains unrestricted, ​Malaysians are advised to consider postponing non-essential trips until the situation improves.

The Malaysian embassy in Paris has issued an advisory urging citizens already in France to exercise caution and remain vigilant.

The US State Department issued an alert on Monday warning Americans to avoid demonstrations in major French cities, while an alert issued by the American embassy in Paris noted new curfews ordered in cities including Paris and Lille.

"Avoid the areas of the demonstrations," the warning said.

And in Europe, some of France's direct neighbors have also issued travel advice to citizens.

The German Foreign Ministry said ‌further riots couldn't be ruled out and urged German nationals to follow instructions from local police. It warned citizens that they could face fines if they fail to adhere to requests to leave unauthorized demonstrations.

Governments in the Czech Republic, the Netherlands, Poland, Denmark, Sweden, ​Finland and Norway also issued warnings to avoid protests.

Skip next section Albania: Prime Minister Rama says protesters crossed 'red line'

Albania: Prime Minister Rama says protesters crossed 'red line'

Albanian Prime Minister Edi Rama said on Monday that protesters had crossed a "red line" after a police station was set ablaze during anti-government demonstrations.

"Protests are a right, whereas violence is a crime," Rama wrote on social media. "This red line must be drawn clearly at this critical stage of our democratic development."

Demonstrators in Albania have been clashing with police since last Tuesday after months of protests over university conditions and political corruption came to a head.

Fresh unrest broke out again in the capital Tirana on Monday evening, with protesters throwing Molotov cocktails at the interior ministry and riot police responding with water cannons, tear gas and rubber bullets.

Prime Minister Rama said he was prepared to engage in dialogue, but not with those who commit violence or political parties which fail to distance themselves from it.

"Violence is not a solution, but the government also needs to reflect deeply to understand this revolt," one 22-year-old student protester told the AFP news agency.

"We are not criminals; we want social peace and better living conditions in our country. We will continue our movement until Rama resigns."

Around 300 people have reportedly been injured in the clashes, according to local authorities, more than half of them police officers.

Police said they detained 68 people in Sunday's unrest in Tirana, of whom 22 will face prosecution.

Skip next section Italy's Meloni considers curfew after Milan riot

Italy's Meloni considers curfew after Milan riot

Italian Prime Minister Giorgia Meloni was also considering imposing curfews and other measures on Monday night in response to rioting in several Italian cities over the weekend.

Meloni convened an emergency Cabinet meeting to discuss her government's response, with local media reporting that emergency decrees could be passed as early as Tuesday.

Italy's ANSA news agency reported that the government intends to "respond decisively" after days of peaceful protests against the high cost of living descended into riots and looting in cities including Milan, Turin and Bologna.

On Milan's central cathedral square, young people dressed in black and wearing masks smashed shop windows and looted supermarkets. At least 14 security personnel were injured, according to official figures, with Milanese prosecutors speaking of "rare violence."

In total, more than 270 people were detained, most of them minors.

Many luxury stores in central Milan remained closed on Monday as Italian media drew comparisons with events in France.

Hard-right Prime Minister Meloni has governed in Rome for four years at the head of a coalition of right-wing and conservative parties. Parliamentary elections are due to be held next year.

Skip next section France: Curfews imposed in parts of Paris, Lille, Nice

France: Curfews imposed in parts of Paris, Lille, Nice

French authorities imposed curfews in parts of several cities on Monday night in response to criticism over security failings after cost-of-living and anti-government protests descended into rioting and looting over the weekend.

In the capital, Paris, police issued a curfew around the Place de la Republique and Les Halles from 11 p.m. until 6 a.m. local time (9:00 p.m. to 04:00 UTC) on Tuesday morning, while protests were banned in certain other areas from 8 p.m.

"A police deployment is in place to ensure strict compliance with these measures," read a police statement.

On France's south coast, the mayor of Nice signed an order installing a curfew for minors in the city center overnight while nearby Marseille also banned gatherings and demonstrations.

Sources in Prime Minister Sebastien Lecornu's office told the Reuters news agency that curfews had also been set for minors between 8 p.m. and 6 a.m. over the next two days in the northern city of Lille and the nearby towns of Douai, Wattignies and Denain with the agreement of local mayors.

"My determination to restore order is absolute," Lecornu told reporters, ruling out blanket curfews in Paris but not a potential state of emergency.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to DW's coverage of the continuing civil unrest and protests in France and other European countries.

Curfews were declared in several French cities on Monday evening, including in parts of Paris, as authorities looked to prevent a continuation of protests, rioting and looting.

Stay tuned for more in this blog.

entries.title: Germany news: Siemens warns on AI eliminating entry-level jobs
entries.summary: Young people could lack essential capabilities if routine tasks are taken over by AI, industrial giant Siemens says. This comes Germany agrees to deepen cooperation on AI with US tech giant Nvidia. DW has more.
entries.content:
Germany

Germany news: Siemens warns on AI eliminating entry-level jobs

Published October 20, 2026last updated October 20, 2026

Young people could lack essential capabilities if routine tasks are taken over by AI, industrial giant Siemens says. This comes Germany agrees to deepen cooperation on AI with US tech giant Nvidia. DW has more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • Entry-level jobs involving routine tasks often left to artificial intelligence (AI) are still vital for young people to learn basic skills, according to Siemens
  • Chancellor Merz is hosting an investment summit in Berlin, with AI a main focus
  • Berlin's Left Party, which has been accused of antisemitism, is debating the future of a member who has come under fire for anti-Israel stances

This is a round-up of top stories from and about Germany on Tuesday, October 20, 2026:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section More than €225 billion investment committed at summit — economy minister

More than €225 billion investment committed at summit — economy minister

More than €225 billion ($252.5 billion) has so far been pledged in investments in Germany at a summit in Berlin attended by top business leaders, German Economy Minister Katherina Reiche said on Tuesday.

Reiche did not give any details about the commitments made so far, but told broadcaster Deutschlandfunk that the figure only included deals above a volume of €100 million.

Among those planning to invest in Europe's largest economy is the online retail giant Amazon, which said it intended to pour some €16 billion into Germany next year for various schemes.

The company said these would include "the expansion of data centers and AI infrastructure, high-speed satellite internet through Amazon Leo, new logistics projects across the country, and a major new production slate by Prime Video."

"Germany is a hub of innovation and one of the most attractive investment opportunities in Europe," David Zapolsky, Amazon's chief global affairs and legal officer, was quoted as saying in a statement.

"That is why we have invested more than €100 billion here since 2010, and why we plan to invest an additional €16 billion in 2027. We want German businesses, communities, and creators to have the infrastructure and tools they need to compete and grow."

More than 200 German and international executives from large corporations, investment banks and funds are attending the gathering, entitled the Invest in Germany Summit.

Skip next section Left Party debates measures on Israel-critical state parliamentarian

Left Party debates measures on Israel-critical state parliamentarian

The Left Party in Berlin, which has faced accusations of being antisemitic, is holding a meeting to discuss how to deal with its parliamentarian Vanessa Emde, who has raised controversy with pro-Palestinian statements.

Among other things, Emde has supported the idea that there is no right to exist for states, but only for people — thus seemingly going against Germany's firm support of Israel's right to existence.

Emde has refused to retract any of her statements.

She has also criticized a statement on antisemitism that she had signed along with all other members of the Left's parliamentary party in which the signatories committed to upholding Israel's right to existence.

Emde is to attend the online meeting.

Greens, SPD agree to coalition negotiations

This comes as both the Berlin Green Party and the Social Democrats (SPD) confirmed that they were ready to begin coalition negotiations with the Left Party on forming a joint government in the city-state.

The Left Party is due to decide on the issue on October 31 at a party conference.

The three parties held preliminary discussions on the accusations of antisemitism and links to organized crime leveled at the Left Party before beginning the exploratory talks that precede final coalition negotiations.

The Left Party emerged from September 20 elections in Berlin as the strongest party with 25.7% of the vote.

Both the Greens (14.3%) and the center-left SPD (12.1%) came in behind the conservative Christian Democrats (18.8%), who led a previous coalition in Berlin with the SPD.

The far-right Alternative for Germany (AfD) received 16.3% of the vote, but so far, all other parties are officially refusing to enter into any form of cooperation with it at either federal or state level. 

Skip next section AI cooperation with US' Nvidia announced as investment summit continues

AI cooperation with US' Nvidia announced as investment summit continues

The Invest in Germany Summit in Berlin entered its second and final day on Tuesday after opening the previous evening with a speech by Chancellor Friedrich Merz that included the words: "Germany is open for business."

The summit has already yielded an agreement to deepen cooperation on artificial intelligence (AI) in German industry between Germany and US tech giant Nvidia.

Merz and Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang said the combination of Germany's engineering expertise and cutting-edge AI technology would help strengthen the country's economy over the long term.

More than 200 German and international executives representing large corporations, investment banks and funds are attending the event, with closed-door talks scheduled for Tuesday.

The summit aims to attract foreign investment to Germany. Organizers highlight the country's sound public finances, triple-A credit rating as the only G7 nation to hold one, strong rule of law and leading position in European patent filings.

Despite these advantages, Germany has struggled to attract foreign investment in recent years, with high energy prices and labor costs acting as deterrents.

Government sources say investment will be vital to help bridge gaps in public funding as the country seeks to improve infrastructure and support companies' transition to climate-neutral production.

The summit is also being attended by Economy Minister Katherina Reiche and Finance Minister Lars Klingbeil, who also serves as Merz's deputy.

Skip next section Protesters glue themselves to road outside Rheinmetall plant

Protesters glue themselves to road outside Rheinmetall plant

Nine protesters have glued themselves to the road outside a plant run by defense contractor Rheinmetall in Berlin's Wedding district, police said on Tuesday.

Officers have been trying since the early morning to detach the group, a police spokeswoman said.

She said as many as 90 officers had been deployed to the site, where altogether 11 protesters were gathered.

Rheinmetall is Germany's largest weapons manufacturer.

The plant in Wedding, where production began earlier this year, has been the target of several protests, with climate and social justice activist Greta Thunberg among those participating.

Skip next section Young workers need to develop skills away from AI — Siemens

Young workers need to develop skills away from AI — Siemens

German industrial giant Siemens has warned against eliminating entry-level jobs that are now increasingly left to artificial intelligence (AI), saying young workers could be left without essential skills, including those needed to monitor AI-generated work.

Judith Wiese, the company's chief people and sustainability officer, said that handing certain routine tasks to AI meant that young employees would not gain hands-on experience that could benefit them later in their careers.

Wiese said it was necessary, for example, for software developers to be able to write their own code so they could critically examine the code produced by AI.

"The crucial question is always: What do I need to have done, checked and seen myself to avoid being misled by AI?" she said.

However, Wiese said AI could also help employees acquire skills more quickly, while older colleagues could learn from younger ones who had grown up using AI.

Wiese said it was still too early to say how AI would impact employment.

Noting that Siemens has some 30,000 software engineers, she said: "You can use the additional productivity either to do the same work with fewer people or to do more with the same number of employees."

Wiese also pointed out that AI was speeding up work processes, enabling the exploration of new ideas and creating projects that would not have been possible without it.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

DW''s newsroom in Bonn bids a warm guten Tag to all its readers as a previously balmy October decides to move toward more wintry chill.

As Chancellor Merz hosts an investment conference in Berlin where developments in AI is taking center stage, industrial giant Siemens has warned that the technology does not only bring advantages.

The controversy over alleged antisemitism in Berlin's Left Party, which might well soon lead a leftist coalition in the city-state, continues, with the party itself debating what to do about a member who has expressed strong anti-Israel views.

And people in Germany are likely to face much longer waits for doctors' appointments from next year, according to an organization managing family doctors and therapists across Germany.

Read on here for more on these and other stories with a German slant.

entries.title: Japan probe sets course for Mars moon
entries.summary: The MMX spacecraft is on its way to Mars' moon Phobos to collect surface samples that could help answer long-standing questions about the formation of the Solar System.
entries.content:
October 20, 2026

The MMX spacecraft is on its way to Mars' moon Phobos to collect surface samples that could help answer long-standing questions about the formation of the Solar System.

A Japanese spacecraft successfully set off on a journey to one of Mars' moons late Monday in a race to become the first mission to return samples to Earth and potentially unlock the mysterious origins of the Solar System.

The uncrewed Martian Moons eXploration (MMX) mission is expected to reach Mars in August 2027. It will attempt to collect samples from Phobos, the larger of the planet's two moons, and deploy the German-French rover IDEFIX to explore the surface.

The flagship H3 rocket carrying the MMX probe lifted off into a pitch-black sky from the Tanegashima Space Center at 4:41 a.m. local time (1941 GMT Monday), the Japan Aerospace Exploration Agency (JAXA) said.

Flight controllers burst into applause and jumped to their feet as the spacecraft blasted into space, shaking hands and embracing. Thousands of people tuned in to watch the livestream despite the early hour.

An hour later, JAXA announced that the probe had successfully separated from the H3 rocket and was "beginning its journey towards the Martian system."

"I'd dreamt of this day, so I'm incredibly happy," said JAXA scientist Mari Aida. "Right now I feel really relieved."

The agency also received signals from the spacecraft as expected, confirming it was operating normally.

Making way for science

Scientists hope the probe's discoveries will help lay the groundwork for eventual human exploration.

"The samples from MMX will bring forth paradigm-shifting science on the Mars system for generations to come, especially as NASA prepares to send the first humans to Mars," Nicky Fox, administrator of NASA's Science Mission Directorate, said in a message broadcast on the JAXA live stream.

JAXA also hopes the mission will reveal how Mars and its two moons formed, unlocking a key piece of knowledge about the formation of the Solar System.

One theory holds that Mars' two moons formed after a giant celestial body collided with the planet. Another hypothesis suggests the moons are asteroids captured by Mars' gravity. Confirming either theory would help scientists determine "how a habitable environment for life might have arisen on the terrestrial planets," JAXA said, referring to the four rocky planets closest to the sun.

Probe to reach destination in August 2027

The probe is due to arrive near Mars around August 2027, where it will orbit one of the planet's two natural moons, Phobos.

A French-German rover named IDEFIX, after the dog from the Asterix comic series, will be the first vehicle to travel across Phobos to conduct surface observations and help ensure a safe landing for the Japanese probe. It is no bigger than a microwave oven.

Once MMX arrives on Phobos, it will spend about two hours collecting at least 10 grams of material from the moon's surface before launching back into space. It will also study Mars' other natural moon, Deimos, during a series of flybys before leaving the Martian region in 2030.

Another objective of the mission is to explore the possibility of using Phobos as a "natural space station" by establishing the requirements for a round trip.

Phobos is a lumpy, potato-shaped rock measuring about 22 kilometers (14 miles) across.

The mission, which aims to complete the first round trip to the Martian region, is a collaboration involving US and European space agencies along with several private technology companies.

US and Chinese space agencies have also been competing to become the first to return rock samples from the surface of Mars to Earth. NASA's Perseverance rover, which has been exploring the planet since 2021, has already collected samples. The return mission, however, was canceled by US President Donald Trump's administration after a congressional vote in January.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: India news: Rubio set to hold talks with S Jaishankar
entries.summary: Marco Rubio's talks with Indian FM S Jaishankar come as the two countries struggle to finalise a trade deal. Follow DW for more.
entries.content:
India

India news: Rubio set to hold talks with S Jaishankar

Published October 20, 2026last updated October 20, 2026

Marco Rubio's talks with Indian FM S Jaishankar come as the two countries struggle to finalise a trade deal. Follow DW for more.

Skip next section What you need to know

What you need to know

  • US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to visit the world's largest oil refinery in India's Jamnagar, which is owned by billionaire Mukesh Ambani
  • Cockroach Janta Party leaders remain in custody
  • At least three people were killed in India's northeastern state of Manipur after "militants" open fire at villagers

Here's a roundup of our coverage from India on Tuesday, October 20:

Tired of missing our real-time updates? Click here to add us as a Preferred Source on Google. Then tap the "Star" or "Preferred" to keep DW News at the top of your feed.

Skip next section Rubio lands in Mumbai, set to meet Jaishankar, Mukesh Ambani

Rubio lands in Mumbai, set to meet Jaishankar, Mukesh Ambani

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio landed in Mumbai, for his second official visit to the country this year.

Rubio is on a two-day visit to India and is expected to meet Indian Foreign Minister S Jaishankar and billionair Mukesh Ambani.

According to the Ministry of External Affairs (MEA), Rubio will meet Jaishankar around 4 p.m. local time. He will also pay tribute to the 26/11 memorial at Taj Palace hotel and attend the US @250 event.

Skip next section 'No justification for terrorism,' says Rajnath Singh at SCO

'No justification for terrorism,' says Rajnath Singh at SCO

Speaking at the Shanghai Cooperation Organization (SCO) Council of Heads of Government meeting in Tajikistan, India's Defense Minister Rajnath Singh said there can be no justification for terrorism and no double standards in combating it.

Singh described terrorism as "one of the gravest threats to development" and said it not only costs lives but also harms investment and trade.

"Terrorism radicalises societies and keeps our youth devoid of opportunities that they deserve," Singh said.

He said there can be "no place for those who finance, support or provide safe havens to terrorists. The entire ecosystem of terrorism must be firmly and collectively dismantled," he said.

Singh's remarks came in the presence of Pakistan's Foreign Minister and Deputy Prime Minister Ishaq Dar.

In a post on X, Singh reiterated his message, saying: "Terrorism is a serious threat to peace and development. It not only takes the lives of innocent people but also impacts investment, commerce, and the future of the youth."

Skip next section Two Indians charged with election fraud in US

Two Indians charged with election fraud in US

wo Indian nationals were among 28 green card holders caught by authorities in the United States for alleged election fraud.

According to the US Justice Department, Amandeep Kaur, 30, and Kamlesh Shah, 67, have been charged with fraudulently registering to vote and casting ballots in the November 2024 US elections.

The Justice Department said both have been charged with felonies carrying a maximum sentence of five years in prison.

The investigations were conducted under "Operation Protect the Vote," an effort to combat and root out fraud in US elections and uphold electoral integrity.

In a statement, the Justice Department said Kaur, an Indian national living in Rancho Palos Verdes, California, who is seeking to become a US citizen, fraudulently registered to vote in December 2022 and voted in the November 2024 US election.

Shah, who lives in Sacramento, California, fraudulently registered to vote on the day of the November 2024 general election and voted that day. He is charged by information, the statement said.

Skip next section CJP leaders' custody extended, case transferred to crime branch

CJP leaders' custody extended, case transferred to crime branch

The Delhi Police transferred the case of Cockroach Janta Party (CJP) leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka to the Crime Branch for further investigation.

Das and Ranka were arrested on October 14 for trespassing at the recently delisted Jantar Mantar, a prominent protest site in the heart of Delhi.

The duo's judicial custody, initially set for five days, was extended by two days on Monday.

Delhi Police sought further custody of the two, claiming their release could disrupt "peace and tranquillity."

"We're in an emergency. There is no justice. This is a police court and you see what is happening. Just look at the ground that they have taken," Das yelled from a police van when he appeared in court on Monday.

CJP legal affairs chief Ratna Singh alleged a "deliberate use of delaying tactics" to keep Das and Ranka "behind bars."

She called it an "attempt to stifle dissenting voices" and alleged delays in taking up the case.

Das and Ranka's case has been assigned to the Inter State Cell of the Crime Branch. Police registered two FIRs in connection with the protest.

On Oct. 10, the CJP called for protests demanding the resignation of India's election chief, Gyanesh Kumar, over allegations of vote theft and mass voter deletions during the controversial voter roll revision exercise.

The protests were thwarted by Delhi Police amid heavy barricading, heightened security and mass detentions.

Skip next section Rubio heads to India for talks on trade, energy and emerging technologies

Rubio heads to India for talks on trade, energy and emerging technologies

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is expected to land in Mumbai as he begins his second official trip to India this year and holds talks with Indian Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar.

The meeting between Rubio and Jaishankar is expected to focus on "energy, trade and investment, defense, critical and emerging technologies," according to a report in the Indian newspaper The Indian Express.

During his visit, Rubio is also expected to travel to Jamnagar, in the western state of Gujarat, where he is set to visit billionaire Mukesh Ambani's Reliance oil refinery.

Rubio's trip comes amid tensions in relations between the US and India over visa restrictions and tariff threats.

However, speaking in Samarkand on Monday, Rubio said Washington and New Delhi were "very close" to an agreement. The visit is being seen as part of a US effort to repair ties.

The trip also comes days after the US paused sanctions on Russian oil imports.

Speaking in Samarkand, Rubio also said the US had considered the India-US trade deal when deciding to waive sanctions on Russian oil. India is a major importer of Russian oil.

Rubio said Washington had to juggle multiple factors "including our bilateral relationships with other countries and what they realistically are capable of being able to do in terms of their own energy supplies."

"You also can't unravel the economy of other countries because of one central issue," he said.

Skip next section Welcome to our coverage

Welcome to our coverage

Hello! This is Midhat from DW's New Delhi bureau, bringing you the latest updates from across India.

US Secretary of State Marco Rubio is set to arrive in India, where he'll meet Foreign Minister Subrahmanyam Jaishankar in Mumbai. The visit comes a day after Rubio said trade deal talks between India and the United States are close to being wrapped up.

Meanwhile, in Delhi, Cockroach Janta Party leaders Saurav Das and Ashutosh Ranka will remain in custody after a court extended their judicial custody beyond the initial five-day period. Delhi Police has also transferred the case to its crime branch.

Stay tuned for more updates from India throughout the day.

entries.title: Canada: Alberta rejects separation bid, CBC projects
entries.summary: Voters have decisively rejected a proposal to begin the legal process toward Alberta's independence, dealing a major blow to a movement driven largely by economic grievances.
entries.content:
Canada

Alberta votes to remain part of Canada by wide margin, CBC projects

October 20, 2026

Voters have decisively rejected a proposal to begin the legal process toward Alberta's independence, dealing a major blow to a movement driven largely by economic grievances.

Canada's Alberta province has overwhelmingly rejected a plan to begin the process of seeking independence from Canada.

Canadian Public broadcaster CBC and leading private network CTV projected a decisive victory for the federalist side, with official results showing more than 76% support for remaining in Canada after roughly a third of the votes had been counted.

According to preliminary results from the chief provincial electoral office, Elections Alberta, nearly 77% favored staying with Canada with roughly 1 million votes counted, while 23% supported independence.

"Albertans made a clear choice. They chose unity, to build together, and to take care of each other," Prime Minister Mark Carney said in a statement. "Above all, Albertans chose Canada."

"While votes on all questions continue to be tallied, tonight's results on the defining question of separation mean that Albertans and all Canadians will move forward together with renewed purpose and high ambition."

The nonbinding referendum asked residents whether they wanted to stay in Canada or start the legal steps needed for a future binding vote on separation. Although it was not a full referendum on independence, a victory for separatists would have set in motion further steps to pursue that goal.

The vote marks the first such Canadian independence referendum held outside Quebec, where past independence movements have been driven by language and cultural differences.

Settling the question of independence once and for all?

On Monday, Alberta Premier Danielle Smith posted on social media that, "Albertans have voted for a stronger Canada in a united Canada."

Smith will address Albertans on Tuesday evening about the results of the vote.

Smith, who opposes independence from Canada, was forced to call the vote after pressure from within her United Conservative Party. She said she hoped holding the vote would put the question of breaking away from Canada to rest for good.

Home to the world's fourth-largest oil reserves, Alberta is largely rural and conservative.

Its independence campaign was largely fueled by economic grievances. The oil-rich province is almost double the size of Germany in terms of land mass but is much more sparsely populated, with around 5 million residents. Almost half live in its two main cities, Edmonton and Calgary.

Independence-minded Albertans say too much of their revenue goes to the federal government and that leaders in Ottawa have been unfair to the province over energy and environmental policy.

The push for independence has also been encouraged by US President Donald Trump, who has been sharply critical of Canada, one of America's oldest and most trusted allies. Trump has repeatedly suggested making Canada the 51st US state and launched a trade war that remains ongoing.

In the run-up to the vote, Alberta independence advocates held meetings at the US State Department in Washington, D.C., and received coaching from US Republican political operatives. Trump's treasury secretary, Scott Bessent, called Alberta a "natural partner," while Trump's biggest donor, billionaire Elon Musk, recently posted on X that Alberta "should separate" from Canada.

Monday's result is a significant setback for separatist groups and their supporters and a much-needed win for Prime Minister Mark Carney as he attempts to keep the country unified amid the ongoing trade war with the US.

Edited by: Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Australian MP seriously hurt in suspected car attack
entries.summary: Helen Haines, an independent federal lawmaker, suffered severe injuries in what Australia's prime minister has called a deliberate attack by a man in a car.
entries.content:
Australia

Australian MP Helen Haines loses leg after car attack — media

Published October 19, 2026last updated October 20, 2026

Helen Haines, an independent federal lawmaker, suffered severe injuries in what Australia's prime minister has called a deliberate attack by a man in a car.

An Australian lawmaker struck by a car in an apparently deliberate attack on Monday has lost one of her legs, local media reported, citing sources.

Independent MP Helen Haines underwent surgery overnight after suffering what were described as critical injuries in the incident, with national broadcaster ABC and the daily Sydney Morning Herald reporting on Tuesday that one leg had been amputated.

Counterterrorism investigators have joined a police probe into the incident, which occurred outside Haines' constituency office in Wangaratta, northeast of the Victorian capital, Melbourne.

What do we know about the suspected attack on Haines?

Haines, 65, was hit by an SUV, which police said was a white Toyota, outside her office. She suffered serious injuries, particularly to her lower body.

ABC cited witnesses as saying they heard a bang and then saw a woman pinned between two cars.

The driver, described as a 43-year-old man, has been arrested, according to Prime Minister Anthony Albanese.

Albanese said early investigations suggested the driver made a U-turn before hitting Haines as she was loading or unloading items at the trunk of her car.

"This wasn't an accident. There was a deliberate act, it would appear," he told ABC.

Local barber ran to assist

Local barber Ricky Jeffries, whose shop is next to Haines' office, has been widely hailed as a hero after he ran to pull the driver out of the car and restrained him until police arrived.

Jeffries downplayed his role, despite having intervened in what could have been a highly dangerous situation, as the man had a knife in the car.

"He [the driver] did have a knife. He didn't ​pull it ‌out. I just wasn't comfortable with his movements, and so I basically just took it out of his pocket and threw it away," he said.

Jefferies said he then held the man down until ‌police arrived.

"I just leant over him and once he was on the ground and ‌he was ​no longer a threat, I just stood with him and I told him that he can't leave," he said.

Jefferies told journalists his first thought had been: "My wife would be disappointed if I'm injured."

"The other people here were just, they did so much more than me ... they deserve the credit," he added.

Political violence on the rise: PM Albanese

Albanese said it was too early to speculate about the possible motive behind the suspected attack, but pointed to rising political violence.

"The temperature has increased in recent times," Albanese added, "I've expressed that concern to people in the media."

Ben Carroll, the state premier for Victoria where Wangaratta is located, said he was "appalled" by the attack, adding: "I know how devastating this will be for the Wangaratta community and all those who Helen represents."

At a separate press conference, Albanese said everyone was "praying for her full recovery."

Although it has not yet been established whether the incident was deliberate, there has been an increase in threats and harassment targeting lawmakers and other senior public officials in Australia and elsewhere in recent years.

Haines had worked as a nurse and a midwife before entering parliament in 2019. She is known for her stance on stronger climate action.

Edited by: Karl Sexton and Louis Oelofse

entries.title: Christiane Amanpour to leave CNN after 43 years
entries.summary: Christiane Amanpour's announcement comes after Paramount Skydance's controversial merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, CNN's parent company.
entries.content:
October 20, 2026

Christiane Amanpour's announcement comes after Paramount Skydance's controversial merger with Warner Bros. Discovery, CNN's parent company.

Veteran journalist Christiane Amanpour on Monday said she was leaving her role at CNN after 43 years at the network.

"After thinking carefully for several months and experiencing a few sleepless nights, as you can imagine, I've decided to separate from CNN," Amanpour, 68, said in a statement.

"This daily show on CNN and PBS will come to an end at the end of this year. But CNN and I have worked out a smooth transition where we continue doing Amanpour once a week through to June," she said in a video message posted on social media.

Amanpour, who became famous for her on-the-ground reporting from major war zones, did not give a reason for her departure.

That said, her move to resign comes weeks after CNN's parent company, Warner Bros. Discovery (WBD), was formally taken over by Paramount Skydance.

After a yearlong process, Paramount closed its merger with WBD on October 6, uniting two giants in TV news — CBS and CNN — under one roof.

The merger has drawn concerns over the independence of the newsroom at CNN as the merged company's owners, the Ellison family, are close allies of US President Donald Trump.

"You know I've always been fiercely independent, and I will continue to be that for you as long as I am here and beyond. That's especially important today as we face unprecedented pressures from all sides, political, financial, and also from the rising dangers in the field," she said, without directly referring to the deal.

What to know about Amanpour's career

Amanpour, who was born in London to an Iranian father and British mother, joined CNN in 1983 as an assistant. In the next few years, she went on to cover major wars in the 1990s, including the Gulf War and the Bosnian War.

Amanpour has interviewed many world's leaders, reported from conflict sites and interviewed newsmakers from hotspots such as Iraq, Afghanistan, Pakistan, Somalia, Rwanda and the Balkans.

She said she "looks forward to interesting new projects down the line, and will always be rooting for CNN and maintaining its history of independent journalism. Remember: always be truthful, not neutral."

In a memo, CNN Chief Executive Mark Thompson praised Amanpur for "43 extraordinary years of remarkable journalism, loyalty and friendship."

"Like so many CNNers who will hear the news today, I'm very sorry to see her go, but I've come to accept that this is the right time for her, both personally and professionally," Thompson said.

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar

entries.title: Zelenskyy accuses US of delaying Patriot missile shipment
entries.summary: Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the United States of delaying deliveries of air defense missiles already paid for by European allies, as relations between Washington and Kyiv deteriorate.
entries.content:
Ukraine

Zelenskyy accuses US of delaying Patriot missile shipment

October 20, 2026

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the United States of delaying deliveries of air defense missiles already paid for by European allies, as relations between Washington and Kyiv deteriorate.

Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy has accused the US administration of delaying the delivery of crucial missiles needed by Ukraine to defend itself against Russian attacks. 

He told US senators on Monday that "the Pentagon is delaying the delivery of missiles" even though they had already been paid for by Ukraine's European allies.

The accusations come as Ukraine-US relations are strained. US President Donald Trump has eased sanctions on Russia and directly criticized Zelenskyy, calling for someone else to take his place.

What did Zelenskyy say?

The Ukrainian president said that the US was holding back interceptor missiles, with one shipment only waiting for the signature of US Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth before it could be sent to Ukraine. 

He also said that Ukraine's European allies had agreed to transfer some of their own Patriot missiles but that this too was pending the green light from the US .

"The missiles are ready, and they could already be in Ukraine," Zelenskyy said. "But unfortunately, there is still no approval."

Earlier on Monday, he said Ukraine had again not received any early warnings about incoming Russian missile strikes. The country is dependent on the ability of US intelligence to spot fast-moving ballistic missiles fired by Russia.

There are also growing concerns over restrictions affecting Starshield, a military satellite communications network developed by Elon Musk's SpaceX. Ukrainian military communications and drone operations depend on using Starshield data.

The US government controls access to Starshield, but Trump has denied ordering any restrictions.

US says it's not withholding intelligence

The accusations come as Ukraine faces renewed Russian attacks on its energy infrastructure. In the night between Sunday and Monday, several Russian ballistic missiles struck the Ukrainian capital and its surroundings, cutting off electricity to more than half a million households.

"Another Russian ballistic missile attack came in several waves overnight, and once again, there was no early warning from our partners," Zelenskyy wrote on Telegram about the attack.

The US, though, dismissed claims it was withholding information, with US Secretary of State Marco Rubio insisting that Washington had not paused its intelligence sharing with Kyiv.

On Monday, Trump doubled down on his previous complaints about alleged ingratitude from the Kyiv administration.

"We've given a lot to Ukraine. They've given nothing to us. Remember that," Trump told reporters in Washington on Monday.

Regarding the easing of sanctions and the diesel deal between Washington and Moscow, Donald Trump strongly criticized Zelenskyy for calling out the deal. 

"Zelenskyy doesn't know what he's talking about," Trump said. "To be honest, I think it's time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine."

Edited by: Roshni Majumdar
